document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 34-year-old man is referred after his father died of a myocardial infarction at age 41. On examination he has bilateral thickening of the Achilles tendons, yellow plaques on both eyelids, and a white ring at the corneal margin. Fasting lipids show markedly elevated total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol with normal triglycerides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolemia results from a genetic defect in the LDL receptor (most common), PCSK9, or ApoB, and the main laboratory abnormality is elevated total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and ApoB. Its characteristic clinical features are tendinous xanthomatosis of the Achilles, patellar, and hand extensor tendons, arcus cornealis, and xanthelasmata, with heterozygotes developing premature CAD and men carrying a 50% risk of myocardial infarction by age 30. This patient's tendon xanthomas, xanthelasmata, arcus, isolated LDL elevation, and family history of premature coronary death fit this pattern.

optionExplanations.b: Familial combined hyperlipidemia raises both triglycerides and LDL and presents with premature coronary heart disease, xanthelasma, and obesity, not tendinous xanthomatosis with normal triglycerides.
optionExplanations.c: Familial LPL deficiency causes elevated triglycerides from excess chylomicrons with abdominal pain, lipemia retinalis, and eruptive xanthomata presenting in infancy.
optionExplanations.d: Tangier disease is an autosomal recessive ABCA1 disorder causing low HDL with enlarged orange-coloured tonsils, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and neuropathy.
optionExplanations.e: Familial hypoalphalipoproteinemia produces low HDL cholesterol from an ABCA1 or ApoA1 mutation, not markedly elevated LDL with tendon xanthomas.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with previous coronary stenting takes a maximally tolerated dose of rosuvastatin plus ezetimibe and adheres to a healthy dietary pattern and regular exercise. Fasting lipids show LDL cholesterol 1.7 mmol/L, ApoB 0.65 g/L, and triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L. Which additional pharmacologic therapy is most appropriate to reduce his cardiovascular risk?
questions.explanation: In the treatment intensification approach for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, a triglyceride level of 1.5 to 5.6 mmol/L is the branch point that leads to consideration of icosapent ethyl 2000 mg BID. This patient has established ASCVD on maximally tolerated statin with LDL cholesterol already below 1.8 mmol/L and ApoB below 0.70 g/L, so the residual treatable abnormality is his triglyceride level of 3.2 mmol/L.

optionExplanations.b: PCSK9 inhibitors are considered when LDL cholesterol remains at or above 1.8 mmol/L or ApoB at or above 0.70 g/L on maximally tolerated statin, which is not the case here.
optionExplanations.c: Fibrates are not part of the ASCVD treatment intensification algorithm shown on this page.
optionExplanations.d: Nicotinic acid appears only as a third-line add-on option for polygenic familial hypercholesterolemia, not for residual hypertriglyceridemia in ASCVD.
optionExplanations.e: Bile acid sequestrants are listed only as an alternative LDL-lowering add-on, and this patient's LDL is already at target.

source.reference: E6 — Figure 3c. Treatment Intensification Approach for Patients with ASCVD

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes lives in long-term care with moderate dementia and is dependent for most activities of daily living. Over the past year she has had two episodes of severe hypoglycemia requiring paramedic assistance. Her current A1c is 6.8% on glyburide and metformin. Which glycemic target is most appropriate for her?
questions.explanation: A1c targets should be personalized based on frailty, functional dependence, and life expectancy. Higher A1c targets of 7.1 to 8.5% may be considered in patients with limited life expectancy, greater functional dependency, recurrent severe hypoglycemia, or frail elderly patients with dementia. This woman is functionally dependent, has dementia, and has had recurrent severe hypoglycemia, so relaxing her target is appropriate.

optionExplanations.a: There may be harm associated with strategies targeting an A1c below 6.0%.
optionExplanations.b: An A1c of 6.0 to less than 6.5% is reserved for selected adults with type 2 diabetes who have potential for remission to prediabetes or normoglycemia.
optionExplanations.c: An A1c below 6.5% is targeted in adults with type 2 diabetes at low risk of hypoglycemia to reduce chronic kidney disease and retinopathy risk, which does not describe this patient.
optionExplanations.d: An A1c below 7.0% is the target for most adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, but not for frail, functionally dependent patients with recurrent severe hypoglycemia.

source.reference: E9 — Glycemic Targets / Figure 5. Glycemic Targets for Diabetes

questions.question: A 74-year-old bedridden man with type 2 diabetes is brought from a nursing home after 10 days of increasing lethargy and reduced fluid intake. He is profoundly volume depleted and obtunded, with unlaboured respirations. Glucose is 58 mmol/L, serum osmolality is markedly elevated, bicarbonate is normal, and urine is negative for ketones but positive for glucose. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state occurs in type 2 diabetes and is characterized by hyperglycemia (typically 44.4 to 133.2 mmol/L), hyperosmolality, and dehydration without ketosis, because residual insulin inhibits lipolysis. Onset is insidious with weakness, polyuria, polydipsia, and decreased fluid intake, and dehydration is more severe than in DKA because of the gradual onset in bedridden patients; Kussmaul respirations are absent unless a precipitant causes acidosis. Urine is negative for ketones with glycosuria.

optionExplanations.b: DKA usually occurs in type 1 diabetes with glucose typically 14 to 55 mmol/L, anion gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul respirations, and urine positive for both glucose and ketones.
optionExplanations.c: Euglycemic DKA occurs with near-normal sugars in pregnancy and with SGLT2 inhibitor use, whereas this patient has extreme hyperglycemia without acidosis.
optionExplanations.d: This presentation lacks the ketonemia and metabolic acidosis that define a ketoacidotic state.
optionExplanations.e: Metabolic acidosis is absent, and his bicarbonate is normal.

source.reference: E13 — Table 11. Acute Complications of Diabetes Mellitus: Hyperglycemic Comatose States

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting and abdominal pain. Glucose is 32 mmol/L, pH 7.12, anion gap 28, and serum potassium 3.0 mmol/L. She has received 1 L of normal saline and remains normotensive. The resident asks whether to begin the insulin infusion now. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give 40 mEq/L potassium replacement and withhold insulin until serum potassium is 3.3 mmol/L or higher
Start insulin regular infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h and add KCl 10-40 mEq/L to the fluids
Start insulin regular infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h without potassium replacement
Give one ampoule of sodium bicarbonate over 1 hour, then start the insulin infusion
Add D5W to the intravenous fluids and start the insulin infusion

questions.explanation: In DKA, total body potassium is depleted and insulin administration drives potassium intracellularly, worsening hypokalemia. If serum potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, give 40 mEq/L potassium replacement and hold insulin until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L. This patient's potassium of 3.0 mmol/L is below that threshold, so potassium must be replaced before insulin is started.

optionExplanations.b: Adding KCl 10-40 mEq/L alongside insulin applies when serum potassium is 3.3 to 5.0 mmol/L, not below 3.3 mmol/L.
optionExplanations.c: Insulin should not be used in hypokalemia until serum potassium is corrected to above 3.3 mmol/L.
optionExplanations.d: Bicarbonate is given if pH is below 7.0 or if hypotension, arrhythmia, or coma is present, and should not be given if pH is above 7.1.
optionExplanations.e: Dextrose is added once blood glucose falls to 14.0 mmol/L to maintain glucose at 12-14 mmol/L, not at presentation with glucose of 32 mmol/L.

source.reference: E14 — Table 11. Acute Complications of Diabetes Mellitus: Treatment (DKA)

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes today at a routine visit. She feels well, her blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, and her physical examination is unremarkable. You wish to begin screening for diabetic nephropathy at the time of diagnosis. Which investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Random urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio plus serum creatinine for eGFR
Twenty-four hour urine collection for protein and albumin

questions.explanation: Screening for diabetic nephropathy uses serum creatinine for eGFR plus a random urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, because albuminuria is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy. Screening begins annually at diagnosis for all patients with type 2 diabetes, and more than 5 years after diagnosis for postpubertal patients with type 1 diabetes. Diagnosis requires persistently elevated urinary albumin on 2 of 3 samples over 3 months.

optionExplanations.b: A 24 h urine collection is the gold standard but is difficult to perform, inconvenient, and often incorrect, so it is not used for routine screening.
optionExplanations.c: Random urine albumin alone is insufficient because albumin levels vary with urine concentration.
optionExplanations.d: Renal ultrasound is not part of the recommended nephropathy screening approach.
optionExplanations.e: Renal biopsy is not a screening test for diabetic nephropathy.

questions.question: A 34-year-old operating room nurse without diabetes has recurrent episodes of sweating, tremor, and confusion that resolve promptly with juice. During a supervised episode her blood glucose is 2.1 mmol/L and her serum insulin is elevated. Her physician must determine whether the hyperinsulinemia is exogenous or endogenous. Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: C-peptide is a short peptide released into the circulation when proinsulin is cleaved to insulin, so it is produced only by endogenous insulin secretion. An increased C-peptide indicates an endogenous source of hyperinsulinemia, whereas a decreased or normal C-peptide in the face of high insulin indicates an exogenous source. Measuring C-peptide during the documented hypoglycemic episode therefore separates surreptitious insulin administration from an insulinoma.

optionExplanations.b: Cortisol is assessed when hormone deficiency is suspected as a cause of hypoglycemia, not to determine the source of hyperinsulinemia.
optionExplanations.c: IGF-2 overproduction causes hypoglycemia from non-islet cell tumours, a mechanism that is insulin-independent.
optionExplanations.d: Autoantibodies to insulin or the insulin receptor cause autoimmune hypoglycemia but do not distinguish exogenous from endogenous insulin.
optionExplanations.e: Imaging may localize an insulinoma but does not establish whether the circulating insulin is endogenous.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man reports that over five years his ring size and shoe size have increased. Examination shows coarsened facial features, prognathism, thickened skin, and enlarged hands. He has carpal tunnel syndrome, newly diagnosed hypertension and hyperglycemia, and his partner reports loud snoring with witnessed apneas. Which investigation is the most appropriate first-line test?
questions.explanation: This presentation of acromegaly reflects growth hormone excess after epiphyseal fusion, producing enlargement of hands and feet, coarsened facial features, prognathism, carpal tunnel syndrome, hypertension, diabetes, and sleep apnea. The first-line test for suspected GH excess is serum IGF-1, which is expected to be elevated because GH acts indirectly through hepatic IGF-1.

optionExplanations.b: Serum GH is undetectable for most of the day and secretion remains pulsatile even in GH excess, so a random level is unhelpful.
optionExplanations.c: The glucose suppression test is the most specific test but is not the first-line screening test.
optionExplanations.d: MRI of the sella turcica is needed to look for a tumour once biochemical excess is established, not as the initial test.
optionExplanations.e: Skull x-ray may show cortical thickening and sellar changes but is not the first-line diagnostic test.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has eight months of amenorrhea and bothersome bilateral galactorrhea. Pregnancy test is negative and TSH, creatinine, and liver enzymes are normal. She takes no medications with anti-dopaminergic properties. Serum prolactin is markedly elevated and MRI of the sella turcica shows a 6 mm pituitary adenoma. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: First-line treatment of hyperprolactinemia is a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine, cabergoline, or quinagolide, with surgery plus or minus radiation reserved for rare cases. Cabergoline should be preferentially used because of its higher efficacy in normalizing prolactin levels and shrinking pituitary tumours, and treatment is indicated in symptomatic patients, particularly those with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, low libido, or infertility.

optionExplanations.b: Surgery is reserved for treatment-resistant prolactinomas after the dopamine agonist dose has been increased to the maximal tolerable dose.
optionExplanations.c: Radiation is a rare adjunct and is not initial therapy for a symptomatic microprolactinoma.
optionExplanations.d: Somatostatin analogues are used as second-line therapy for acromegaly, not for prolactinoma.
optionExplanations.e: Levothyroxine would be appropriate only if primary hypothyroidism were driving the prolactin elevation, but her TSH is normal.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man with a large pituitary macroadenoma is investigated for fatigue, weight loss, cold intolerance, and constipation. Free T4 is low with a low TSH, and 8 am cortisol is low with a subnormal cosyntropin stimulation test. His endocrinologist plans replacement of both deficient axes. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?

options.text: Start glucocorticoid replacement first, then add levothyroxine
Start levothyroxine first, then add glucocorticoid replacement
Start levothyroxine and glucocorticoid simultaneously at full replacement doses
Start levothyroxine alone and reassess cortisol in six weeks
Start fludrocortisone first, then add levothyroxine

questions.explanation: Adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism are the two important deficiencies to recognize in hypopituitarism. Concurrent adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism should be treated with glucocorticoids first and then with thyroid hormone in order to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis. Starting thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid is therefore unsafe in this patient.

optionExplanations.b: Giving thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid risks precipitating adrenal crisis.
optionExplanations.c: Simultaneous initiation does not respect the required sequence of glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone.
optionExplanations.d: His cortisol deficiency is already documented and requires replacement, and untreated it may be unmasked by thyroid hormone.
optionExplanations.e: Mineralocorticoid replacement is used in primary adrenal insufficiency; this patient has central (ACTH-dependent) adrenal insufficiency.

source.reference: E23 — Hypopituitarism: Important Deficiencies to Recognize

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman has three weeks of palpitations, fine tremor, heat intolerance, and weight loss. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Her thyroid is not enlarged, there is no bruit, and she has no eye signs. She is not pregnant. Which investigation best determines whether her thyrotoxicosis is due to gland overproduction or to hormone leak?
questions.explanation: Radioactive iodine uptake is a test of function that should be ordered when a patient is thyrotoxic, because it measures turnover of iodine by the thyroid in vivo. Increased uptake indicates the gland is overproducing hormone, as in Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goitre, or toxic adenoma, whereas decreased uptake indicates the gland is leaking hormone (thyroiditis) or that there is exogenous thyroid hormone or an iodine load. RAIU is contraindicated in pregnancy, which has been excluded here.

optionExplanations.b: Free T3 should only be measured in the small subset of patients with suspected T3 toxicosis and does not identify the mechanism.
optionExplanations.c: Thyroglobulin is used to monitor for residual thyroid tissue after thyroidectomy as a tumour marker, and is low when endogenous production is suppressed by exogenous hormone.
optionExplanations.d: Ultrasound measures gland size and characterizes nodules; it is not a test of thyroid function.
optionExplanations.e: Calcitonin is ordered when medullary thyroid cancer is suspected and is not routinely used for thyroid nodules or thyrotoxicosis.

source.reference: E26 — Table 15. Summary of Diagnostic Testing in Hyperthyroidism and Hypothyroidism

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has 10 days of anterior neck pain radiating to the jaw and ears, preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection. She has fever, malaise, myalgia, palpitations, and tremor. The thyroid is exquisitely tender to palpation. TSH is suppressed with elevated T4 and T3, ESR is markedly elevated, and radioactive iodine uptake is near absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Painful subacute (de Quervain's, granulomatous) thyroiditis is presumed to follow a viral infection and is often preceded by a URTI. Thyroid inflammation damages follicles, releasing large amounts of stored T4 and T3, producing painful thyroid swelling that may radiate to the jaw and ears with malaise, fatigue, myalgia, and fever. Laboratory findings are initially elevated T4 and T3 with near-absent RAIU, and in classical painful subacute thyroiditis the ESR is increased.

optionExplanations.b: Painless thyroiditis produces thyroid enlargement without discomfort, so pain, tenderness, and fever would not be expected.
optionExplanations.c: Graves' disease shows increased RAIU with homogeneous diffuse uptake on scan and positive TRAb, not near-absent uptake.
optionExplanations.d: Toxic multinodular goitre shows increased, heterogeneous uptake on scan.
optionExplanations.e: Toxic adenoma shows intense uptake in a single hot nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland.

source.reference: E29 — Table 18. Painful vs. Painless Subacute Thyroiditis

questions.question: A 78-year-old man with stable angina and a prior myocardial infarction reports several months of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and hoarseness. He weighs 70 kg. TSH is 22 mU/L and free T4 is low. Physical examination shows bradycardia, dry skin, and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Levothyroxine 0.025 mg PO daily, increasing gradually every 6 weeks
Levothyroxine 0.112 mg PO daily (full weight-based replacement)

questions.explanation: Overt primary hypothyroidism is treated with L-thyroxine, and the usual full replacement dose is estimated as 1.6 micrograms/kg/day. However, elderly patients and those with coronary artery disease should start at 0.025 mg daily and increase gradually every 6 weeks (start low, go slow), with TSH reassessed 6 weeks after initiation and dose adjusted until TSH normalizes. This 78-year-old man with known coronary disease therefore requires a low starting dose.

optionExplanations.b: Full weight-based dosing of about 1.6 micrograms/kg/day is inappropriate as a starting dose in an elderly patient with coronary artery disease.
optionExplanations.c: 0.2 mg daily is the top of the usual dose range and far exceeds a safe starting dose here.
optionExplanations.d: The recommended replacement agent is L-thyroxine, the synthetic analogue of T4.
optionExplanations.e: Combination therapy is not the recommended treatment for primary hypothyroidism on this page.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman has one year of central weight gain, a rounded plethoric face, purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, and proximal muscle wasting. She has new hypertension and hyperglycemia. A careful medication history confirms she has taken no glucocorticoids in any form. Which investigation is the most appropriate initial biochemical test?

options.text: Late night salivary cortisol on two occasions

questions.explanation: After excluding exogenous glucocorticoid exposure with a thorough drug history, the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome requires at least one of: 24 h urine free cortisol (at least 2 tests), a low dose dexamethasone suppression test, or late night salivary cortisol (at least 2 tests), with confirmation by one of the remaining tests. Late night salivary cortisol measured twice is therefore an appropriate initial screening test in this patient.

optionExplanations.b: A random serum cortisol is not one of the accepted screening tests for Cushing's syndrome.
optionExplanations.c: Plasma ACTH helps classify the syndrome as ACTH-dependent or independent only after hypercortisolism is biochemically confirmed.
optionExplanations.d: Sellar imaging is used to localize a pituitary source, not to establish the presence of cortisol excess.
optionExplanations.e: Adrenal imaging localizes an adrenal source and does not establish the biochemical diagnosis.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman with known Addison's disease has had two days of vomiting and has been unable to take her oral medications. She is confused, with blood pressure 78/44 mmHg and heart rate 122 bpm. Sodium is 126 mmol/L, potassium 5.9 mmol/L, and glucose 3.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: IV normal saline 1 L within the first hour plus hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
IV normal saline 1 L within the first hour alone
Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose for several days

questions.explanation: This is an acute adrenal crisis, which can be life-threatening. Treatment is IV normal saline 1 L within the first hour followed by continuous IV normal saline guided by patient requirements, with D5W added if hypoglycemic, together with hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat followed by 50 mg IV q6 h, while the precipitating factor is identified and corrected.

optionExplanations.b: Fluid resuscitation alone does not replace the absent glucocorticoid and will not reverse the crisis.
optionExplanations.c: Oral therapy is inappropriate in a vomiting, hypotensive, confused patient and provides a maintenance rather than a crisis dose.
optionExplanations.d: Fludrocortisone is maintenance mineralocorticoid replacement for primary adrenal insufficiency, not crisis therapy.
optionExplanations.e: Increasing steroids two to three fold is the stress dosing strategy for moderate to severe illness, not for established adrenal crisis with hypotension.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has episodic pounding headaches, palpitations, and diaphoresis with paroxysmal hypertension. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and CT of the abdomen shows a 4 cm right adrenal mass. Surgical resection is planned in three weeks. Which pharmacologic preparation is most appropriate to begin now?
questions.explanation: Surgical excision of a pheochromocytoma is curative but requires adequate preoperative preparation. Alpha-blockade for blood pressure control with doxazosin or phenoxybenzamine is the most frequently used approach and is started 10 to 21 days preoperatively, with volume restoration by vigorous salt loading and fluids. Beta-blockade is added only if needed for heart rate control once the patient has been alpha-blocked for a few days.

optionExplanations.b: Beta-blockade should only follow several days of established alpha-blockade.
optionExplanations.c: Propranolol is a beta-blocker and is not appropriate before alpha-blockade has been established.
optionExplanations.d: Calcium channel blockade is not the recommended preoperative preparation described for pheochromocytoma.
optionExplanations.e: Metyrosine, a catecholamine synthesis inhibitor, is used together with an alpha blocker rather than alone.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is admitted with confusion, constipation, and reduced urine output. He is clinically dehydrated. Corrected serum calcium is 3.8 mmol/L and creatinine is normal. Aggressive isotonic saline rehydration has been started. Which additional treatment is most appropriate to lower his calcium?

options.text: Subcutaneous calcitonin as the sole additional agent

questions.explanation: A corrected calcium above 3.5 mmol/L is severe hypercalcemia requiring urgent correction because of the risk of dysrhythmia and coma. After fluids, bisphosphonates are the treatment of choice: zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over 15 min or pamidronate 60-90 mg IV over 2 h, which inhibit osteoclastic bone resorption, and IV pamidronate or zoledronic acid are specifically indicated in malignancy-related hypercalcemia.

optionExplanations.b: A loop diuretic is added only if the patient is hypervolemic with urine output above 200 mL/h, and is a temporary measure; this patient is dehydrated and oliguric.
optionExplanations.c: Corticosteroids are used for hypercalcemia mediated by 1,25 vitamin D, such as lymphoma or granulomatous disease.
optionExplanations.d: Calcitonin gives only a transient, partial response with tachyphylaxis after 48 h and is given in conjunction with a bisphosphonate rather than alone.
optionExplanations.e: Dialysis is a treatment of last resort indicated in severe malignancy-associated hypercalcemia with renal insufficiency or heart failure; his creatinine is normal.

source.reference: E44 — Table 29. Treatment of Acute Hypercalcemia/Hypercalcemic Crisis

questions.question: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman fractures her distal radius after tripping from standing height. DEXA shows a lumbar spine T-score of -2.7. Calcium corrected for albumin, phosphate, creatinine, ALP, TSH, and 25-OH vitamin D are all normal. Alongside dietary calcium, vitamin D, and exercise, which drug therapy is most appropriate first line?
questions.explanation: This woman has osteoporosis by BMD (T-score at or below -2.5) plus a fragility fracture from a fall from standing height. Bisphosphonates are first line in the prevention of hip, nonvertebral, and vertebral fractures with Grade A evidence, specifically alendronate PO, risedronate PO, and zoledronic acid IV. Alendronate is therefore the appropriate initial pharmacotherapy.

optionExplanations.b: Raloxifene has evidence for prevention of vertebral fractures only and is a second-line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis.
optionExplanations.c: Teriparatide is given for 18-24 months and must be followed by long-term antiresorptive therapy; it is not the first-line agent.
optionExplanations.d: Romosozumab is a 12-month sclerostin inhibitor course reserved for high fracture risk rather than initial therapy.
optionExplanations.e: Calcitonin is used for Paget's disease when bisphosphonates cannot be tolerated and is not a first-line osteoporosis therapy.

source.reference: E47 — Table 34. Treatment of Osteoporosis in Women and Men

questions.question: A 47-year-old man with type 1 diabetes uses a basal-bolus regimen with basal insulin at bedtime and rapid-acting insulin before breakfast, lunch, and dinner. His glucose log shows readings of 12-14 mmol/L every morning before breakfast, while his lunch, supper, and bedtime readings are all at target. He has had no nocturnal hypoglycemia. Which insulin adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Change to a pre-mixed insulin regimen, two-thirds before breakfast and one-third before dinner

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes pairs each hyperglycemic reading with a specific insulin correction: a high AM sugar is corrected by increasing bedtime basal insulin, a high lunch sugar by increasing AM rapid/regular insulin, a high supper sugar by increasing lunch rapid/regular insulin or AM basal insulin, and a high bedtime sugar by increasing supper rapid/regular insulin. This man's only elevated value is his fasting morning glucose, so the bedtime basal insulin should be increased.

optionExplanations.b: Increasing the AM rapid/regular insulin is the correction for a high lunch sugar, which is already at target.
optionExplanations.c: Increasing the lunch rapid/regular insulin is the correction for a high supper sugar.
optionExplanations.d: Increasing the supper rapid/regular insulin is the correction for a high bedtime sugar.
optionExplanations.e: A pre-mixed regimen is an alternative insulin regimen, not the targeted correction for isolated high AM sugars, and it gives less flexibility for basal titration.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and established heart failure takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily. His A1C remains above target at 8.4% and further glucose lowering is required. His eGFR is 65 mL/min/1.73 m2 and he has had no severe hypoglycemia. Which antihyperglycemic agent should be added?
questions.explanation: When A1C is above target in a person with established cardiovascular or renal disease, Toronto Notes directs adding or substituting an antihyperglycemic agent with demonstrated cardiorenal benefits. For heart failure, SGLT2i (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) are the agents with proven benefit and lower rates of hospitalization for heart failure in outcome trials; they may be initiated if eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2, which this man meets.

optionExplanations.b: Sitagliptin is a DPP4i with CV safety but no proven cardiorenal benefit in high-risk populations.
optionExplanations.c: Saxagliptin is a DPP4i carrying a risk of heart failure and is a poor choice in this patient.
optionExplanations.d: Exenatide ER is a GLP1-RA with CV safety but no proven cardiorenal benefit, unlike dulaglutide, liraglutide, and semaglutide.
optionExplanations.e: Acarbose lowers glucose but has no demonstrated cardiorenal benefit in outcome trials.

source.reference: E15 — Figure 9. Treatment Approach for Patients Living with Diabetes

questions.question: A 51-year-old sedentary man living in Canada attends a periodic health review. Waist circumference is 108 cm and blood pressure is 138/88 mmHg. Fasting bloodwork shows triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L, HDL-cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L, and fasting glucose 6.0 mmol/L. He takes no medications and has no chest pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Isolated elevated waist circumference without metabolic syndrome
Syndrome X related to angina pectoris with normal coronary arteries

questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome is a postulated syndrome related to insulin resistance associated with hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, HTN, central obesity, and dyslipidemia, and 3 of 5 measures are required for the diagnosis. In Canada and the USA the thresholds for men are waist circumference >102 cm, TG >=1.7 mmol/L, HDL-C <1.0 mmol/L, blood pressure >=130/85 mmHg, and fasting glucose >=5.6 mmol/L. This man meets all five measures.

optionExplanations.b: A fasting glucose of 6.0 mmol/L meets the metabolic syndrome threshold of >=5.6 mmol/L but does not establish diabetes here.
optionExplanations.c: Elevated waist circumference is only one of the five measures; he meets four others as well.
optionExplanations.d: His triglyceride elevation is modest and occurs with four other components, which defines a clustered metabolic disorder rather than an isolated lipid disorder.
optionExplanations.e: Metabolic syndrome is not to be confused with syndrome X related to angina pectoris with normal coronary arteries; he has no angina.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with small cell carcinoma of the lung is admitted with headache, nausea, and muscle cramps. He is euvolemic with no edema. Serum sodium is 121 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 68 mEq/L, and urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg. Adrenal, renal, and thyroid function are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The diagnostic criteria for SIADH are hyponatremia (serum Na <135 mEq/L) with plasma hypo-osmolality (<275 mOsm/kg), urine Na concentration >40 mEq/L, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, euvolemia with no edema, and absence of adrenal, renal, or thyroid insufficiency. Ectopic ADH production by tumours including small cell carcinoma of the lung is a listed cause, and this man satisfies every criterion.

optionExplanations.b: Cerebral salt wasting mimics the findings of SIADH but its hallmark is hypovolemia, and it typically occurs after subarachnoid hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.c: Central DI causes passage of large volumes of dilute urine with hypernatremia, not concentrated urine with hyponatremia.
optionExplanations.d: Nephrogenic DI reflects collecting tubules resistant to ADH and again produces large volumes of dilute urine.
optionExplanations.e: Psychogenic polydipsia is excluded by his concentrated urine osmolality of 480 mOsm/kg and high urine sodium.

source.reference: E22 — Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman is found to have a 2.5 cm firm nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid. She has mild palpitations and has lost weight. TSH is 0.01 mU/L and free T4 is elevated. There is no neck pain and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Which investigation is most appropriate to guide management of this nodule?
questions.explanation: U/S is the first line tool for identification of thyroid nodules that require FNAB, but the stated exception is hyperthyroid patients with thyroid nodules, where a radioisotope thyroid scan (Technetium-99) and RAIU identify hyperfunctioning nodules, which generally do not need to be biopsied. A hot nodule carries a very low chance of malignancy and treatment is directed at the hyperthyroidism, whereas a cold nodule requires further workup with U/S then FNAB if sonographic features are concerning.

optionExplanations.b: FNAB is the pathway for a nodule in a euthyroid patient; here the scan must first determine whether the nodule is hot, in which case biopsy is generally unnecessary.
optionExplanations.c: Serum calcitonin is not routinely done to investigate thyroid nodules and is ordered when MTC is suspected, such as in MEN 2A or 2B or a pathogenic RET mutation.
optionExplanations.d: Plasma thyroglobulin is used to monitor for residual thyroid tissue post-thyroidectomy and for thyroid cancer recurrence, not to characterize a new nodule.
optionExplanations.e: TPOAb are increased in Hashimoto's disease and are a normal variant in 10-20% of individuals; they do not characterize a nodule.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who is 8 weeks pregnant has uncontrolled hyperthyroidism and needs an antithyroid medication. She has had no rash, pruritus, hepatitis, or agranulocytosis, and her liver enzymes are normal. Radioactive iodine is not an option and she declines thyroidectomy during the pregnancy. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: The thionamides PTU and MMI inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by inhibiting peroxidase-catalyzed reactions, and PTU also inhibits peripheral deiodination of T4 to T3. In pregnancy Toronto Notes directs use of PTU during the first 16 wk of pregnancy and MMI after: MMI is contraindicated in the first trimester due to the risk of aplasia cutis, while MMI is preferred in the second and third trimesters given the potential risk of hepatotoxicity with PTU then. At 8 wk she should receive PTU.

optionExplanations.b: MMI is contraindicated in the first trimester because of the risk of aplasia cutis, although it is preferred after 16 wk.
optionExplanations.c: Thyroid ablation with radioactive I-131 is contraindicated in pregnancy.
optionExplanations.d: Symptomatic treatment with beta-blockers controls adrenergic symptoms but does not inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis.
optionExplanations.e: Prednisone is used for ophthalmopathy and severe orbitopathy, not for control of thyroid hormone synthesis.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man is in the ICU on day 6 of treatment for severe illness from septic shock requiring vasopressors. He has no known thyroid disease and takes no thyroid medication. Thyroid testing shows a low free T3, a low TSH, and a low-normal free T4. He is normothermic, alert, and has no goitre. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Non-thyroidal illness describes changes in the regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and in thyroid hormone metabolism and transport among patients with severe illness, trauma, surgery, or starvation, and is not due to intrinsic thyroid, pituitary, or hypothalamic disease. The characteristic sequence is an initially decreased free T3 followed by decreased TSH and, if severe illness, decreased free T4, with TSH transiently high on recovery. Treatment is of the underlying disease; thyroid hormone replacement has not been shown to be beneficial.

optionExplanations.b: This pattern is not due to intrinsic pituitary or hypothalamic disease; thyroid function tests normalize once the patient is well.
optionExplanations.c: An intrinsic thyroid defect would raise TSH, whereas his TSH is low.
optionExplanations.d: Decreased mental status and hypothermia are the hallmark features of myxedema coma; he is alert and normothermic.
optionExplanations.e: A toxic multinodular goitre causes hyperthyroidism with a raised free T4 and a nodular gland, neither of which is present.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man has hypertension that remains uncontrolled on three antihypertensive agents. He has no Cushingoid features and no paroxysmal symptoms. His physician suspects a mineralocorticoid excess syndrome such as an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma (Conn's syndrome) and has held the medications known to interfere with testing. Which investigation is the most appropriate screening test?

options.text: Low-dose overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
IV infusion of 500 mL/h of normal saline for 4 h with measurement of plasma aldosterone

questions.explanation: A positive screen for primary aldosteronism is an elevated aldosterone:renin ratio in the presence of a high aldosterone, and multiple medications that interfere with screening and confirmatory tests may need to be held prior to testing. Confirmation of PA then requires demonstrating lack of aldosterone suppression with expansion of ECFV.

optionExplanations.b: The low-dose overnight DXM suppression test screens for hypercortisolism by testing pituitary-adrenal suppressibility, not aldosterone excess.
optionExplanations.c: The cosyntropin stimulation test diagnoses glucocorticoid deficiency by measuring stimulated plasma cortisol.
optionExplanations.d: ECFV expansion with normal saline is the confirmatory test performed after a positive screen; plasma aldosterone >277 pmol/L is consistent with PA.
optionExplanations.e: Elevated 24 h urine free cortisol demonstrates overproduction of cortisol, not aldosterone.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man has two years of epigastric pain from recurrent peptic ulcers and esophagitis. He has had two episodes of nephrolithiasis, and serum calcium and PTH are both elevated. He also describes erectile dysfunction and decreased libido; MRI shows a pituitary adenoma and PRL is markedly elevated. His father had similar problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MEN 1 is an autosomal dominant neoplastic syndrome on chromosome 11 that affects the 3 Ps: pituitary, parathyroid, and pancreas. Primary hyperparathyroidism occurs in about 95% and causes nephrolithiasis and symptoms of hypercalcemia, entero-pancreatic tumours such as gastrinoma cause epigastric pain from peptic ulcers and esophagitis, and prolactinomas are the most common functional pituitary tumour in MEN 1, producing erectile dysfunction and decreased libido. His father's history fits the autosomal dominant inheritance.

optionExplanations.b: MEN 2A involves medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and primary parathyroid hyperplasia, not pituitary or entero-pancreatic tumours.
optionExplanations.c: MEN 2B involves MTC, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas with intestinal ganglioneuromas, and a marfanoid habitus.
optionExplanations.d: Familial MTC is MTC without other clinical manifestations of MEN 2A or MEN 2B.
optionExplanations.e: A sporadic parathyroid adenoma would explain the hypercalcemia and stones but not the gastrinoma or the prolactinoma.

source.reference: E41 — Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia / Table 26. MEN Classification

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman feels well but routine bloodwork shows a total corrected serum calcium of 2.88 mmol/L, confirmed on repeat testing. PTH is elevated and serum phosphate is low. She takes no medications, including no lithium or thiazide diuretics, has no history of malignancy, and her chest x-ray is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy mediated by PTHrP

questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia is defined as a total corrected serum Ca2+ >2.6 mmol/L, and the initial investigation is PTH. A normal or high PTH with a low phosphate identifies primary hyperparathyroidism, which is due to a solitary adenoma in 81%, hyperplasia in 15%, and carcinoma in 4%. The PTH-independent causes of hypercalcemia sit on the low PTH branch of the differential.

optionExplanations.b: Humoral mediation by PTHrP produces hypercalcemia with a low PTH and a low phosphate, and she has no malignancy.
optionExplanations.c: Hypervitaminosis D from excessive intake of vitamin D or its metabolites raises calcidiol with a suppressed PTH.
optionExplanations.d: Granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis, sarcoid, or lymphoma causes extra-renal production of calcitriol by macrophages with a low PTH; her chest x-ray is normal.
optionExplanations.e: Milk alkali syndrome is hypercalcemia with metabolic alkalosis and renal insufficiency and suppresses PTH.

source.reference: E43 — Hypercalcemia / Figure 20. Differential Diagnosis of Hypercalcemia

questions.question: A 33-year-old man is investigated for decreased libido, sparse facial hair, and gynecomastia. Testes are small and firm. Two morning fasting total testosterone measurements are below the laboratory reference range, confirming the diagnosis of hypogonadism. LH and FSH are both high, and semen analysis shows azoospermia. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: In the diagnostic approach to testosterone deficiency, a low total testosterone is confirmed by repeating the morning fasting measurement, after which LH and FSH are measured. High LH and FSH indicate primary hypogonadism from primary testicular failure, and the next step is to obtain a karyotype to diagnose Klinefelter syndrome when there is a clinical indication. His small firm testes, gynecomastia, and azoospermia are that indication.

optionExplanations.b: Pituitary MRI is part of the workup when LH and FSH are low or inappropriately normal, indicating secondary hypogonadism.
optionExplanations.c: Prolactin is measured in secondary hypogonadism to look for hyperprolactinemia as a reversible functional cause.
optionExplanations.d: Iron saturation is measured in secondary hypogonadism to look for hemochromatosis.
optionExplanations.e: The diagnosis of hypogonadism is already confirmed by two low morning fasting total testosterone measurements.

source.reference: E52 — Figure 24. Diagnostic Approach to Testosterone Deficiency

questions.question: A 68-year-old man started on spironolactone six months ago reports bilateral breast enlargement with mild pain. Examination shows concentric, rubbery, firm tissue extending from each nipple that is not fixed to underlying tissue, with no skin dimpling or retraction and no nipple discharge. Testes are normal in size and there are no stigmata of liver disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Gynecomastia due to a testicular germ-cell neoplasm

questions.explanation: True gynecomastia is benign proliferation of the glandular component of the male breast, forming a concentric, rubbery, firm mass extending from the nipple that is not fixed to underlying tissue. Drugs such as spironolactone, cimetidine, digoxin, ketoconazole, and antiandrogens are listed causes, acting through decreased androgen activity or increased estrogen activity. His examination and the temporal relation to spironolactone make drug-induced gynecomastia the most likely diagnosis.

optionExplanations.b: Pseudogynecomastia or lipomastia is enlargement of soft adipose tissue, especially in obese individuals, rather than the firm rubbery glandular tissue described.
optionExplanations.c: Red flags for breast cancer are a unilateral, eccentric, hard or fixed mass, skin dimpling or retraction, and nipple discharge or crusting, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: Cirrhosis causes gynecomastia through reduced ability of the liver to metabolize and inactivate estrogens, but he has no stigmata of liver disease.
optionExplanations.e: Testicular and germ-cell neoplasms cause gynecomastia, but his testes are normal on examination.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with untreated Graves' disease develops a temperature of 40.2°C, heart rate 148 with atrial fibrillation, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, and delirium two days after emergency surgery. Free T4 and T3 are elevated with an undetectable TSH. She receives fluids, a cooling blanket, acetaminophen, propranolol, and a high dose of propylthiouracil. One hour later, which medication should be added to acutely inhibit the release of thyroid hormone?

options.text: Sodium iodide 1 g IV drip over 12 h

questions.explanation: For thyroid storm the source directs that iodide, which acutely inhibits the release of thyroid hormone, be given 1 h after the first dose of PTU — sodium iodide 1 g IV drip over 12 h q12h, or Lugol's solution, or SSKI. This woman has extreme hyperthermia, tachycardia with atrial fibrillation, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, and delirium after surgery, and has had her first high dose of PTU one hour ago, so iodide is the agent to add now.

optionExplanations.b: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h is given for the first 24-48 h, but it works by inhibiting peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 rather than blocking hormone release.
optionExplanations.c: Methimazole in high doses is an alternative thionamide that blocks hormone production; she has already received PTU, the traditional preferred choice.
optionExplanations.d: Propranolol has already been given for adrenergic control and decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3; it does not block release of stored hormone.
optionExplanations.e: Dexamethasone, like hydrocortisone, inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and is not the agent given 1 h after the first dose of PTU.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man with biopsy-proven small cell lung cancer describes three months of muscle weakness in his limbs, with difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Strength does not fluctuate through the day and there is no ptosis. Memory and orientation are intact and he has had no seizures. Sodium is 138 mmol/L and potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. CT shows a hilar mass with no thymic enlargement. What is the most likely paraneoplastic syndrome?
questions.explanation: The source classifies Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome as a neurologic paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung cancer that presents with muscle weakness in limbs, produced by antibody that interferes with acetylcholine release. Myasthenia gravis is listed instead with thymoma and with fluctuating muscle weakness and fatigability. This man has small cell lung cancer, limb weakness that does not fluctuate, and no thymic enlargement, so LEMS is the best fit.

optionExplanations.b: Myasthenia gravis is the thymoma-associated syndrome in this table and causes fluctuating muscle weakness and fatigability; his CT shows no thymic enlargement.
optionExplanations.c: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis also accompanies small cell lung cancer but presents with depression, seizures, and short-term memory loss, none of which he has.
optionExplanations.d: SIADH from small cell lung cancer causes oliguria and hyponatremia with nausea, headache, and confusion; his sodium is normal.
optionExplanations.e: Hypokalemic nephropathy from ectopic ACTH secretion presents with polyuria, polydipsia, anorexia, and vomiting; his potassium is normal.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is referred after routine bloodwork showed a serum alkaline phosphatase three times the upper limit of normal with a normal GGT and otherwise normal liver enzymes. He has aching pain in his right femur and pelvis, and his right tibia appears bowed. Serum calcium and phosphate are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Plain x-ray of the skull, abdomen, and tibiae
Serum procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP)

questions.explanation: The source recommends plain x-ray of the skull and facial bones, abdomen, and tibiae as the initial screening study in patients suspected of having Paget's disease of bone, and states that confirmation on x-ray is required for diagnosis. Paget's disease should be considered in older adults with an elevated ALP but normal GGT and normal LFTs, and this man also has severe bone pain in the pelvis and femur with a bowed tibia. X-ray shows the characteristic osteolytic lesions, cortical thickening, and pseudofractures.

optionExplanations.b: A bone scan is recommended to evaluate the extent of disease and identify asymptomatic sites, but in addition to targeted x-ray rather than as the initial study.
optionExplanations.c: MRI is not recommended for diagnosis; it is used to assess disease complications, particularly if malignancy is suspected.
optionExplanations.d: CT is likewise not recommended for diagnosis and is reserved for assessing complications.
optionExplanations.e: Elevated PINP is a bone formation marker that supports increased turnover, but confirmation on x-ray is required for diagnosis.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man who had a pituitary lesion resected two years ago is assessed for infertility after 18 months of unprotected intercourse. He reports decreased libido and reduced muscle mass. Total testosterone and follicle stimulating hormone are low, and his sperm count is zero on two samples. He wishes to father a child. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: hCG with recombinant follicle stimulating hormone (rFSH)
GnRH agonist given SC in pulsatile fashion using an external pump

questions.explanation: When the goal is fertility, the source treats the underlying cause and gives hCG with or without recombinant follicle stimulating hormone in cases of either hypothalamic or pituitary lesions, reserving a pulsatile GnRH agonist for hypothalamic dysfunction with an intact pituitary. This man's low testosterone, low FSH, and absent sperm follow resection of a pituitary lesion, so gonadotropin therapy is the appropriate treatment.

optionExplanations.b: A GnRH agonist administered SC in pulsatile fashion by an external pump is used for hypothalamic dysfunction with an intact pituitary, which he does not have.
optionExplanations.c: Testosterone therapy only treats symptoms of hypogonadism and further suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, decreasing spermatogenesis and reducing sperm counts.
optionExplanations.d: A dopamine agonist such as cabergoline is indicated when the cause is a prolactinoma.
optionExplanations.e: Testicular sperm extraction is used only if the testicular tissues are not functioning, which is not the problem here.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man is referred for fatigue and diffuse bronze discolouration of the skin. Examination shows hepatomegaly, no facial plethora or purple striae, and no enlargement of the hands or feet. He is not overweight and takes no medications. Fasting plasma glucose is 9.8 mmol/L on two occasions. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his diabetes?
questions.explanation: The source classifies diabetes caused by diseases of the exocrine pancreas separately from type 1 and type 2 disease, and lists pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis, and hemochromatosis ("bronze diabetes") in that group. Bronze skin discolouration with hepatomegaly in a man who is not overweight and has new hyperglycemia fits hemochromatosis. The absence of cushingoid features, acral enlargement, and any drug exposure argues against the endocrinopathies and drug-induced causes on the same list.

optionExplanations.b: Acromegaly is listed as an endocrinopathy that can cause diabetes, but there is no enlargement of the hands or feet.
optionExplanations.c: Cushing's syndrome is also on the endocrinopathy list, yet he has no facial plethora or purple striae.
optionExplanations.d: Glucocorticoids head the drug-induced causes of diabetes, and he takes no medications.
optionExplanations.e: Klinefelter's syndrome is among the genetic syndromes associated with diabetes but does not produce bronze skin and hepatomegaly.

source.reference: E8 — Etiologic Classification of Diabetes Mellitus

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman with minimal sun exposure has several months of diffuse skeletal pain, bone tenderness, and a waddling gait with proximal muscle weakness. Radiographs show narrow radiolucent lines traversing both femoral necks. Serum calcium is 2.05 mmol/L, serum phosphate is decreased, and serum alkaline phosphatase is increased. Serum creatinine and bicarbonate are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
Osteomalacia due to proximal renal tubular acidosis

questions.explanation: The source gives diffuse skeletal pain, bone tenderness, fractures, waddling gait, and proximal muscle weakness as the clinical features of osteomalacia, and describes pseudofractures (Looser zones) as narrow radiolucent lines on x-ray. Among the causes, only vitamin D deficiency shows decreased serum phosphate with decreased-to-normal serum calcium and increased ALP; hypophosphatemia and proximal renal tubular acidosis both leave serum calcium normal. A frankly low calcium with normal creatinine and no acidosis therefore points to vitamin D deficiency.

optionExplanations.b: Hypophosphatemia gives decreased phosphate and increased ALP, but serum calcium remains normal.
optionExplanations.c: Proximal renal tubular acidosis shows decreased phosphate with normal calcium and normal ALP, and is associated with hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, which she does not have.
optionExplanations.d: Renal osteodystrophy is bone disease secondary to chronic kidney disease, and her serum creatinine is normal.
optionExplanations.e: Conditions associated with abnormal matrix formation, such as fibrogenesis imperfecta ossium, have normal phosphate, calcium, and ALP.
